newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian Cera holds breath despite strong 1996.
newsitem.headline: Belgian Cera holds breath despite strong 1996.

text.p: Belgian Cera Bank said on Thursday its 1996 consolidated net profit soared 71 percent but warned that it and other banks were bracing for tougher times.

"Luckily every (bank) has recorded excellent 1996 results because we're facing a period which is going to cost us quite a bit of money," said Cera chief executive officer Willy Breesch, who is also chairman of the Belgian Banking Association.
Breesch told a news conference on 1996 earnings that the direct cost of the Euro introduction for Belgian banks would be 20 billion francs over the next four to five years.
In addition banks were to lose 20 billion francs due to the loss of forex trading commission income.
Banks would also lose money from revising and updating computers by the turn of the century.
Many older computers record only the last two digits of a year to track dates and could treat the year 2000 as the year 1900 -- the so-called millennium bug.
But the bug and Euro would also weigh on another level.
"These operations also have a very big opportunity cost," Breesch said.
He said the fact that computer scientists would have to focus entirely on the Euro and millennium bug would stop them from further developing banks' other activities.
"All new commercial activities will have problems," he said.
The unlisted Cera Bank group had a 1996 consolidated net profit of 5.78 billion francs against 3.38 billion a year earlier.
